newsitem.title: USA: Tensions ease in Texas standoff.
newsitem.headline: Tensions ease in Texas standoff.

text.p: A tense three-day standoff between police and armed Texas separatists holed up in a mountain compound appeared to be nearing a peaceful end on Tuesday, authorities said.

But even as police expressed optimism that the siege was about over, they turned up the heat on the Republic of Texas group by bringing in a pair of armoured personnel carriers to complement elite SWAT (special weapons and tactics) teams already in place in the rugged Davis mountains of west Texas.
Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox told reporters that telephone negotiations to end the standoff were going well.
"We're optimistic there's going to be a peaceful outcome to all this," he said. "We've had a good dialogue going on and things are looking very positive."
Terence O'Rourke, attorney for Republic leader Richard McLaren, agreed, saying, "We could wrap this up today."
"(McLaren) does not have a death wish, he does not need to be a martyr. His cause and his integrity could be well served by his getting out alive," O'Rourke said.
Neither he nor Cox would disclose the nature of the negotiations. Cox said police believe there are 13 people, all adults, barricaded inside the tin-walled compound.

The Republic of Texas formed in late 1995 and claims to have thousands of members and ties to anti-government militias. It wants Texas to secede from the United States and become an independent nation, as it was for nine years after breaking away from Mexico in 1836.

The standoff began on Sunday when Republic members grabbed two hostages from a nearby home in retaliation for the arrest of their security chief, Robert Scheidt, on charges he had illegal weapons. One of the hostages, Joe Rowe, was injured when the Republic members shot their way into his house.

The hostages were released on Monday in a swap for Scheidt, but charges of aggravated kidnapping and engaging in an organised criminal activity were filed against six of the Republic members. The charges carry penalties of up to 99 years.

Dozens of state, local and federal police have poured into the remote area about 200 miles (320 km) southeast of El Paso, Texas. SWAT teams have moved to within two miles (3.2 km) of the compound, which Cox said may be helping negotiations.
"He is aware we have slowly moved in his direction," he said of McLaren.

McLaren was charged with contempt in December for failing to appear in federal court on charges related to bogus liens issued by the Republic. Since then he and several followers have holed up inside the compound, sending out their separatist message by fax and the Internet.
Police, fearful of touching off the anger of militia groups, have not attempted to arrest him for the earlier charge, but Texas Attorney General Dan Morales said on Tuesday the situation had changed.

"Members of this group are no longer novelties or curiousities, they now are bona fide criminals. What is occurring in west Texas is terrorism, pure and simple," he told a news conference in Austin, Texas.

Cox said the two 13-tonne armoured personnel carriers were supplied by Sheriff J.B. Smith of Smith County in east Texas. Smith told Reuters last week he had recently obtained them under a federal programme giving old military equipment to civilian police forces. He named the two vehicles "Bubba 1" and "Bubba 2."
